title: Directories: ReadDir, WalkDir, path vs path/filepath, os.Root
summary: os.ReadDir lists one level and filepath.WalkDir a whole tree, both in byte order. Use path for "/" names, path/filepath for OS paths, and os.Root (Go 1.24) to open user-supplied names without escaping a directory.

examples.title: ReadDir for one level, WalkDir for a tree, io/fs for "/" names

annotations.note: MkdirAll is mkdir -p: it creates missing parents and succeeds if the directory already exists. Forward slashes work in os calls on Windows too; paths you get back from filepath use backslashes there.

ReadDir returns fs.DirEntry values sorted by name as bytes: uppercase Z before lowercase n, and İ (0xC4 0xB0) after every ASCII letter. Fine for deterministic output, wrong for a Turkish user's list, which needs collation (golang.org/x/text/collate).
A non-nil err means WalkDir couldn't read path (permissions, a vanished directory). Returning it stops the whole walk; returning nil skips that directory and carries on.
fs.SkipDir on a directory skips its subtree without reading it, so node_modules costs nothing. fs.SkipAll (Go 1.20) ends the walk early without an error.
filepath.WalkDir hands you OS paths: data\raporlar\Ocak.csv on Windows. ToSlash makes the printed form the same everywhere.

os.DirFS("data") is the same directory as an fs.FS. Names are relative to it and always use "/", which is what embed.FS, zip archives and fstest.MapFS use too, so code written against fs.FS works with all of them.

examples.title: path vs path/filepath, Join, IsLocal and Localize

annotations.note: The path package is pure string manipulation with "/" on every OS. Use it for URL paths and io/fs names; using it on Windows file paths would mishandle backslashes and drive letters.
filepath uses the OS separator. Rel computes the path of p relative to "data". Printing through ToSlash keeps the output identical on Windows and Linux.
Join calls Clean, which resolves ".." lexically. With a name taken from a request, uploads/../../etc/passwd becomes ../etc/passwd: Join is not a security boundary.

IsLocal (Go 1.20) is true only for a non-empty, relative name that stays inside the directory it is joined to; a/../b stays inside, so it passes. It checks the string only: a symlink inside the tree can still point outside.

Localize (Go 1.23) takes an io/fs-style name, as in a URL, and gives an OS path, or an error for names that aren't valid fs paths (.., leading /) or that the OS can't represent, such as a\b on Windows.

examples.title: os.Root keeps every lookup inside one directory

annotations.note: OpenRoot (Go 1.24) opens the directory once and keeps a handle to it. Every method on root resolves names relative to that handle and refuses any step that leaves it.
Writes stay inside as well. Names such as kasım are UTF-8 strings in Go; on Windows the os package converts them to the UTF-16 the system calls expect, so the same code works on both.
The naive Join plus os.ReadFile leaks secret.env twice. root.ReadFile refuses both: ".." may not climb above the root, and neither may absolute names or symlinks that point outside it.

use_cases: Listing a folder for a UI or an API: os.ReadDir
Indexing, cleanup and import jobs over a tree: filepath.WalkDir with SkipDir for vendor and node_modules
Serving or reading user-named files (uploads, report downloads, archive extraction): os.Root or os.OpenInRoot
Code that should work on disk, in embed.FS, in a zip and in tests: accept an fs.FS
strengths: WalkDir avoids an lstat per entry (unlike the older filepath.Walk), and DirEntry.Info only stats when you ask
Deterministic order out of the box: ReadDir and WalkDir sort by name, unlike Node's fs.readdir or Python's os.scandir, which return directory order
os.Root resolves names with openat-style lookups, so it is safe against symlink tricks that a lexical check like IsLocal (or Java's normalize().startsWith()) misses
weaknesses: Two path packages that look alike; mixing them up compiles and fails only on Windows
Byte-order sorting is wrong for display: İ, Ç, Ş sort after z
os.Root confines names, not resources: it doesn't stop bind mounts, /proc files or device files on Unix, as its docs say

pitfalls.title: filepath.Join as a sandbox
pitfalls.detail: Join cleans .. away from the result; it never refuses. Use os.Root (or at least filepath.IsLocal) for names that come from users, archives or URLs.

pitfalls.title: path where filepath was meant
pitfalls.detail: path.Join("C:\\data", "x") treats the whole "C:\\data" as one name. Use filepath for anything the OS opens, path for URLs and fs.FS names.

pitfalls.title: Case-insensitive file systems
pitfalls.detail: NTFS (Windows) and macOS's default APFS treat Rapor.csv and rapor.csv as one file; Linux ext4 sees two. Code that dedupes or looks up names behaves differently in Docker than on your machine.

pitfalls.title: Returning err from the WalkDir callback by reflex
pitfalls.detail: One unreadable directory then aborts the whole walk. Decide: stop, or log and return nil to skip it.

quiz.why: Join cleans the result lexically. It doesn't confine anything, which is why user-supplied names need os.Root or IsLocal.

quiz.q: Which package do you use to join the parts of a URL path or an embed.FS name?
options: either; they're the same on Linux
quiz.why: URL and io/fs names always use "/". filepath would produce backslashes on Windows.

quiz.q: filepath.IsLocal(name) is true. Is opening filepath.Join(dir, name) now safe against escaping dir?
options: Only lexically: a symlink inside dir can still lead outside
quiz.why: IsLocal checks the string. os.Root checks each step against the real file system, symlinks included.

body:
## Concept

- `os.ReadDir(dir)` reads one directory and returns `[]os.DirEntry` (an alias of
  `fs.DirEntry`), sorted by name. A `DirEntry` knows its name and type from the directory
  read; `Info()` fetches size and times only if you call it.
- `filepath.WalkDir(root, fn)` visits a whole tree in lexical order, calls `fn` for every
  directory and file, and lets `fn` prune with `fs.SkipDir` or stop with `fs.SkipAll`.
  It doesn't follow symbolic links.
- `path` handles `"/"`-separated names (URLs, `io/fs`, `embed.FS`, zip entries) on every
  OS; `path/filepath` handles the OS's own paths, with `\` and drive letters on Windows.
- `os.Root` (Go 1.24, with `MkdirAll`, `ReadFile`, `WriteFile`, `Rename` and more in 1.25)
  opens a directory and then refuses any name that would leave it, through `..`, an
  absolute path or a symlink.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C: `opendir`/`readdir` plus `nftw`; `os.Root` is the `openat`-relative-to-a-dirfd
  discipline, wrapped so every method uses it.
- Java: `Files.list` and `Files.walk` (lazy streams, unsorted) vs Go's sorted slices.
  `path.normalize().startsWith(base)` is the lexical check that `filepath.IsLocal` replaces,
  with the same symlink blind spot.
- Python: `os.scandir` ≈ `os.ReadDir` (both avoid a stat per entry), `os.walk` ≈ `WalkDir`,
  `posixpath` vs `os.path` ≈ `path` vs `filepath`.
- Node: `fs.readdir(dir, { withFileTypes: true })` ≈ `ReadDir`; `path.posix` vs `path` ≈
  `path` vs `filepath`. Node has no equivalent of `os.Root`.

## How it works

`os.Root` resolves a name one component at a time from the directory handle it holds (on
Unix with `openat(2)` and `O_NOFOLLOW`, following symlinks itself). `..` may not climb
above the root, a leading `/` (or `C:` on Windows) is rejected, and symlinks are followed
only if they are relative and their target stays inside. Because it never builds a full
path string and then opens it, there is no gap between "checked" and "opened" for an
attacker to swap a directory for a symlink (the docs list the few exceptions, such as
`Root.Chmod` on Unix). On Windows it also refuses reserved device names such as `NUL` and
`COM1`. `root.FS()` gives the same protection behind the `fs.FS` interface; `os.DirFS`
does not, as its own documentation warns.

## Design notes

Keep the OS at the edge. Functions that only read files can take an `fs.FS`, and `main`
decides whether that is `os.DirFS(dir)`, `root.FS()`, an `embed.FS` or a zip archive;
tests pass a `fstest.MapFS`. For anything that turns user input into a file name (download
endpoints, upload storage, archive extraction), open an `os.Root` once at startup for the
directory and route every access through it; `filepath.IsLocal` is a good input check but
not a substitute. Sort for display with locale-aware collation, and remember that the same
two names can be one file on your Windows machine and two in the Linux container.
